answer:
The WHO World Malaria Report 2024 estimated 263 million malaria cases and 597,000 malaria deaths worldwide in 2023 [1]. That was about 11 million more cases than in 2022 and nearly the same number of deaths [1]. About 95% of the deaths occurred in the WHO African Region [1]. Since 2000, an estimated 2.2 billion malaria cases and 12.7 million deaths have been averted [1].

The report covers efforts in 83 countries [1]. It introduced, for the first time, a dedicated chapter on inequity, focusing on populations most vulnerable to malaria, including children under 5, women and girls, Indigenous Peoples, migrants, people with disabilities, and people in remote areas with limited healthcare access [1].

The report also highlighted positive trends in the scale-up of prevention tools, including new generation nets, malaria vaccines, and seasonal malaria chemoprevention [5]. Regional data showed that increases in cases and deaths from 2021–2022 were mainly due to the malaria situation in Papua New Guinea, linked to low treatment seeking and testing rates, stock-outs of commodities, human resource and management constraints, and unstable sources of domestic funding [4].
